# Average mass and length plot
![](/images/elephant.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"}

Now let's compare the average weight and length.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(x = animal_df$`Average mass (tonnes)`,
     y = animal_df$`Average total length (m)`)
```
:::


With that we can see the following:

- At lower weights (< 20 tonnes) a longer length does not necessarily mean a higher mass
- At higher weights (>20 tonnes) there appears to be an overall trend of longer lengths equaling higher masses with the animal with the highest mass having the longest length

## Plot section zoom
![](/images/zoom.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"}

It is quite hard to see the overall trend in the lower mass animals as they are squashed in a small part of the plot. We can zoom into this part in two different ways.

The first method is to limit the x and y axes, allowing us to choose the part of the plot to zoom into.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(x = animal_df$`Average mass (tonnes)`,
     y = animal_df$`Average total length (m)`,
     xlim = c(0,10), ylim = c(0,10))
```
:::


The second method is to subset the data that is plotted.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(x = animal_df[animal_df$`Average mass (tonnes)` < 10,
                   "Average mass (tonnes)"],
     y = animal_df[animal_df$`Average mass (tonnes)` < 10,
                   "Average total length (m)"])
```
:::


I personally prefer the x and y limit approach.

## Colour points by metadata
![](/images/coloured_points.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"}

We can also include the Biom metadata as an aesthetic in the plot.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
#Plot
plot(x = animal_df$`Average mass (tonnes)`,
     y = animal_df$`Average total length (m)`, 
     col = as.numeric(animal_df$Biom),
     pch = 1
     )
#Legend
legend(x = "bottomright", col = 1:nlevels(animal_df$Biom), 
       legend = levels(animal_df$Biom), pch = 1)
```
:::
